title: Fifteen Years of Produce Safety Rules, and Outbreaks Keep Coming
hook: The FDA wrote real rules for how farms grow your salad. The problem is almost nobody checks whether farms follow them — some have never had a single inspection.
key_points: The Food Safety Modernization Act, passed 15 years ago, set federal safety standards for produce farms.
Farms must follow rules on hand-washing, irrigation water quality, compost and manure handling, and discarding produce near animal feces.
Enforcement is the weak link: most farms get no regular government inspection, and some have never been inspected at all.
NPR reports the Taylor Farms facility tied to the 2026 cyclospora outbreak had gone about seven years without an inspection.
Longtime FDA adviser Jim Gorny said inspecting farms 'once every three years would be ideal' — monthly is 'not possible.'
Investigators also still can't always pin down where an outbreak started, so rules alone can't close the gap.
content_html: Fifteen years ago the FDA overhauled how fruits and vegetables are grown in the U.S., writing federal safety standards into the Food Safety Modernization Act. Farms are supposed to follow rules on worker hand-washing, the quality of irrigation water, how compost and manure are handled, and throwing out produce found near animal feces. It's a genuine regulatory framework. NPR's Jeff Guo asked the obvious follow-up question: is it working?
extra_html:
The answer NPR lands on is that the rules are only as good as the checking, and the checking barely happens. Most produce farms receive no regular government inspection. Some, 15 years in, still haven't had their first one. Jim Gorny, a longtime FDA adviser, told NPR that inspecting a farm "once every three years would be ideal," while conceding that anything like monthly visits is "not possible" with the resources available. Sharpening the point: NPR reports the Taylor Farms facility linked to the record cyclospora outbreak of summer 2026 had gone roughly seven years without an inspection.

There's a scientific limit too. Even with a traceback investigation running, officials often can't say with certainty where a contaminated batch came from — as the cyclospora outbreak showed when the FDA had to retract its one positive lab test. The practical takeaway isn't that the rules are worthless; it's that they aren't a guarantee. Outbreaks still arrive unpredictably, which is why the boring advice — wash your hands, wash your produce, follow recall notices — is still the part you control.

related.title: A Record Cyclospora Outbreak With an Elusive Source
related.hook: A Cyclospora outbreak has now topped 4,100 cases — a U.S. record — even after the FDA retracted its lone positive lab test, leaving Taylor Farms lettuce as the prime suspect on epidemiology alone.

related.title: Food Safety at Home
related.hook: Most food poisoning starts in an ordinary kitchen. Four simple habits — clean, separate, cook, chill — prevent the great majority of it.

related.title: Handwashing: The Cheapest Medicine
related.hook: It sounds almost too simple, but washing your hands well is one of the most effective things you can do to stop the spread of illness in a household.

flashcards.prompt: Fifteen years after the FDA's produce safety overhaul, what does NPR identify as the main weakness?

choices.text: Enforcement — most farms get no regular inspection, and some have never been inspected
The rules themselves were never written
Farms are inspected too often, driving up food prices

flashcards.explanation_html: The standards exist — hand-washing, irrigation water quality, manure handling. What's missing is anyone checking. Most farms see no regular government inspection, and some still haven't had a first one.

flashcards.prompt: Name two things the FDA's produce safety rule actually requires of farms.
flashcards.back_html: Any two of: hand-washing protocols for workers, irrigation water quality standards, proper compost and manure handling, and removing produce found near animal feces.

flashcards.prompt: Why don't these rules mean you can stop washing your produce?
flashcards.back_html: Because compliance largely goes unchecked and investigators often can't trace an outbreak's source with certainty. Outbreaks keep happening unpredictably, so the basics — wash your hands, wash your produce — still fall to you.
